lessonTitle: Working Within Limits and Raising Concerns: Competence, Speaking Up and Incident Reporting

blocks.text: In your second week as a doctor a nurse tells you that the registrar has asked you to insert a chest drain for a patient, because 'you did one as a student'. You watched a drain being inserted once, and the registrar is in theatre. You could do what you are told and hope for the best, or say 'I am not competent to do this unsupervised'. Only one of those answers protects the patient, and it takes more courage than the procedure.

blocks.markdown: A foundation doctor works within a system of supervision and is expected to know the edges of their competence. The General Medical Council's guidance in Good medical practice asks doctors to recognise and work within the limits of their competence and to ask for help when needed. This is not a weakness; it is a core patient-safety skill. The same professional duty extends to **speaking up** when you see a risk to patients and to **reporting incidents and near misses** so that systems can learn. Check the current version of the GMC guidance and your own trust's policies.

blocks.title: Competence and supervision
blocks.text: Competence is the ability to do a task safely and effectively to an accepted standard, and depends on knowledge, skill and judgement, and on the situation (for example, you may be competent to cannulate a calm patient but not a shocked, uncooperative one). Supervision is the level of oversight a task requires, from direct supervision with a senior present to indirect supervision with a senior available on the phone; the Foundation Programme uses defined supervision levels, so check your programme's current rules.

rows: Asked to do a procedure you have not been trained or signed off for
Say you are not competent alone, ask for supervision or a trained colleague, and arrange the safest alternative meanwhile
Attempt it because refusing feels awkward
Unsure of a diagnosis or plan
Discuss with a senior, using SBAR, and document the advice
Asked to consent a patient for a procedure you do not understand
Decline and ask someone who can explain the risks and alternatives
Obtain a signature to complete the form
Tell your supervisor or nurse in charge, ask for help or reduced workload
Clarify politely and, if unresolved, escalate and do not act against your judgement of safety
blocks.caption: Working within limits: what to do and what to avoid.

blocks.title: Responding to a request beyond your competence
blocks.prompt: At 23:00 a nurse asks you to perform an ascitic tap on a 58-year-old man with alcohol-related liver disease who has tense ascites and abdominal discomfort. You have never done one, the registrar is in theatre and the patient is currently stable. What do you do?

steps.text: Assess the situation honestly: the procedure is outside your competence, the patient is stable and the risk is non-immediate, so there is time to arrange proper supervision.
Say clearly to the nurse and patient that you have not been trained to do this alone and that you will arrange it safely; do not attempt it in the hope of coping.

Contact your senior with SBAR: 'I have a patient with tense ascites needing a diagnostic or therapeutic tap; I am not trained to do this alone; can you or another competent doctor supervise or do it, and when?'
Make interim arrangements: continue observations, review clotting and platelet results, ensure consent will be obtained by someone who understands the procedure, and plan a time.
Document your assessment, the discussion, the plan and the time, and reflect afterwards on what training you need, using the learning to plan supervised practice.

blocks.answer: Refuse to perform it unsupervised, escalate promptly, keep the patient safe in the meantime and document; seek supervised training later.

blocks.markdown: **Raising a patient safety concern.** A concern might be a single unsafe act, a faulty piece of equipment, repeated staffing gaps or a colleague's behaviour that puts patients at risk. The general approach in UK practice is: (1) act at once if a patient is in immediate danger; (2) raise the concern promptly with the person responsible or the relevant senior, such as your supervisor, the nurse in charge or the clinical lead; (3) use local routes such as the incident reporting system and the Freedom to Speak Up Guardian; (4) if the concern remains unresolved or is serious, escalate to a senior leader such as the medical director, and then to external bodies such as a regulator (for example the Care Quality Commission or the General Medical Council); (5) record what you saw and did, factually and with dates. In the UK the Public Interest Disclosure Act 1998 protects workers who make a protected disclosure, broadly a qualifying disclosure made in the right way to the right person with a reasonable belief that it is in the public interest; check the details with your trust's policy or professional body.

items: Protect the patient first: stop, check, or ask for urgent help.
Say what you saw in factual, specific terms, without speculating about motives.
Raise it promptly with the relevant person: supervisor, nurse in charge or clinical lead.
Report on the incident system and use the Freedom to Speak Up Guardian if you need support.
If the concern persists, escalate to senior management and then to an external route, documenting each step.

blocks.title: Raising a concern about missed observations
blocks.prompt: Over three nights you notice that a ward's four-hourly observations are repeatedly missed for patients who have been flagged as at risk. No harm has yet occurred. Explain how to raise the concern.

steps.text: Treat any at-risk patient now: check that those currently overdue are measured, and escalate any abnormal observations to the nurse in charge.
Collect facts: which nights, how many observation sets were missed, which patients, and what staffing was recorded, without blaming individuals.

Raise the issue at once with the nurse in charge and with your consultant or clinical supervisor, using SBAR: 'On three nights I found that observations were not done for patients flagged as at risk, and I am worried about missed deterioration.'
Submit an incident report describing the pattern, because a trend is only visible if it is reported, and record that the concern was raised.

Follow up: ask what action will be taken, use the Freedom to Speak Up Guardian if there is no response, and if the risk remains escalate to the medical director or a regulator; legal protection under the Public Interest Disclosure Act generally depends on a qualifying disclosure made in the right way to the right person with a reasonable belief that it is in the public interest; check your policy.

blocks.answer: The concern is raised early, factually and through more than one route, with escalation if there is no response and documentation at each step.

blocks.markdown: **Incident reporting and a learning culture.** An **incident** is any unintended event that caused or could have caused harm. A **near miss** is an event that did not reach the patient or did not cause harm, but could have. Reporting near misses is valuable because the same system weaknesses lie behind them as behind harmful events. In England, patient safety events are reported locally and then shared nationally through the Learn from Patient Safety Events service; check which system your trust uses. A **just culture** (rather than a blame culture) examines the system factors behind an error, treats honest mistakes as opportunities to learn and reserves individual accountability for reckless or deliberately unsafe behaviour. Doctors also have a professional duty of candour, meaning they should be open and honest with patients when something goes wrong and apologise; check current General Medical Council and Nursing and Midwifery Council joint guidance. Organisations in England also have a statutory duty of candour (Care Quality Commission Regulation 20); check current regulations.

blocks.title: Why reporting matters
blocks.text: James Reason's 'Swiss cheese' model describes harm as the result of several holes in different layers of defence lining up. A near miss shows that one layer failed and another caught it, so reporting it helps to close holes before they line up again. A ward with no incident reports is not necessarily safe; it may be one where people do not feel safe to speak.

blocks.caption: Incidents per 1000 bed-days allows wards of different sizes to be compared; a higher rate of reported near misses often indicates a healthy reporting culture, not worse care.

blocks.title: Comparing reporting rates
blocks.prompt: Ward A reported 12 falls incidents during 4000 occupied bed-days. Calculate the rate per 1000 bed-days and explain how you would interpret it.

steps.text: Write the formula: rate = number of incidents divided by bed-days, multiplied by 1000.
Evaluate the fraction and scale: 12 divided by 4000 is 0.003, and multiplying by 1000 gives 3.
State the result with units: 3.0 incidents per 1000 occupied bed-days.

Interpret carefully: compare with the ward's own past rates and with similar wards, look at severity and whether near misses are being reported, and use the data to find learning rather than to blame staff. A rise might reflect better reporting or a real problem, so review the incidents themselves.

blocks.answer: 3.0 incidents per 1000 bed-days; the figure is a prompt for review of causes and trends, not a verdict.

blocks.title: Blame discourages reporting
blocks.text: If staff expect punishment for honest mistakes, they hide them and the organisation loses the chance to learn. In a just culture, you report promptly, tell the patient, and reflect, and the investigation looks first at the system rather than the person.

points: Recognise your limits, ask for help early and say so plainly; asking is a professional duty, not a weakness.
Raise concerns promptly and factually: protect the patient, speak to the responsible senior, use the incident system and the Freedom to Speak Up Guardian, and escalate externally if needed.
Report incidents and near misses; a just culture looks at system causes and holds individuals accountable only for reckless behaviour.
Incident rates per 1000 bed-days help compare wards, but should be interpreted with context.

questions.stem: A surgical registrar asks you to obtain consent from a patient for an operation. You do not know what the procedure involves or its main risks. What should you do?

options.text: Ask the patient to read the form and sign it alone
Complete the form with generic risks copied from another patient
Decline, explain why, and ask someone who understands the procedure to consent the patient
Obtain the signature using the standard consent form so the list is not delayed

questions.correctOptionText: Decline, explain why, and ask someone who understands the procedure to consent the patient

distractorRationale.a: Does not provide information or the chance to ask questions.
distractorRationale.c: Correct: you must understand what you are consenting for.
distractorRationale.d: Consent without understanding is invalid and unsafe.

questions.explanation: Valid consent requires a clinician who understands the procedure, its risks and alternatives and can discuss them. Working within your competence means declining and ensuring that a suitably informed colleague takes consent.

questions.stem: At 02:00 a nurse asks you to insert a central venous catheter into a stable patient because the cannula has failed. You have never done this and your senior is on call at home. What is the best response?

options.text: Ask the nurse to do it
Explain your limits, call the senior for advice or supervision, and arrange the safest interim access you are competent to use
Attempt the line anyway since you have seen it done
Refuse and leave the problem for the day team without telling anyone

questions.correctOptionText: Explain your limits, call the senior for advice or supervision, and arrange the safest interim access you are competent to use

distractorRationale.a: Not within the nurse's role or yours to delegate if untrained.
distractorRationale.b: Correct: protects the patient and shows insight.
distractorRationale.c: Seeing a procedure is not competence.
distractorRationale.d: Fails to arrange care and is unsafe.

questions.explanation: You can recognise your limit and still act responsibly by phoning the senior, who can supervise, come in or advise an alternative. A stable patient allows time for this, and you should document the discussion and plan.

questions.stem: A foundation doctor who asks a senior colleague for help with a task beyond their competence is showing poor professional performance.

options.text: True
False

questions.explanation: Recognising the limits of your competence and seeking help is a professional duty set out in Good medical practice, and it protects patients. Failing to ask is the greater risk.

questions.stem: You see a colleague give a medicine without checking the patient's identity band, and a patient could have been given the wrong drug. What is the best initial action?

options.text: Wait until the next appraisal to mention it
Say nothing because the patient seems well
Post about it on social media
Make sure the patient is safe now, then raise the issue promptly with the relevant senior or supervisor and report it using the incident system

questions.correctOptionText: Make sure the patient is safe now, then raise the issue promptly with the relevant senior or supervisor and report it using the incident system

distractorRationale.b: Silence prevents learning and may allow harm to recur.
distractorRationale.d: Correct: patient safety first, then speaking up and reporting.

questions.explanation: The first duty is the immediate safety of the patient, followed by prompt, factual reporting through the right channels. Social media and silence are both inappropriate.

questions.stem: You raised a serious patient safety concern with your consultant six weeks ago and nothing has changed. The risk remains. What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Wait until you leave the placement
Drop the matter because you have raised it once
Escalate through local routes such as the Freedom to Speak Up Guardian or medical director and, if unresolved, to an external body, documenting each step
Confront the consultant in front of the team

questions.correctOptionText: Escalate through local routes such as the Freedom to Speak Up Guardian or medical director and, if unresolved, to an external body, documenting each step

distractorRationale.a: Leaves patients at risk in the meantime.

questions.explanation: If an initial concern is not resolved, guidance expects you to take it higher and, where needed, outside the organisation to a regulator or other prescribed body, while documenting what you did. Legal protection for disclosures depends on following the correct route, so check your trust's policy.

questions.stem: Which description best fits a near miss?

options.text: An event that was not noticed by anyone
An event that could have caused harm but was caught or did not reach the patient
An event that only involved equipment being out of date
An event that caused permanent harm to a patient

questions.correctOptionText: An event that could have caused harm but was caught or did not reach the patient

distractorRationale.a: A near miss is, by definition, recognised.
distractorRationale.b: Correct: a near miss is a prevented or non-harmful event.
distractorRationale.c: Not necessarily; a near miss is defined by potential for patient harm.

questions.explanation: A near miss is an event with potential to cause harm that did not do so, often because another safeguard worked. These events are useful because they reveal system weaknesses without any patient being hurt.

questions.stem: A medical ward records 15 medication incidents, including near misses, over 6250 occupied bed-days. Calculate the reporting rate in incidents per 1000 bed-days.
questions.explanation: The rate is the number of incidents divided by bed-days, multiplied by 1000: 15 / 6250 x 1000 = 2.4 incidents per 1000 bed-days. Rates standardise wards of different sizes, though a higher reporting rate may reflect a better safety culture rather than poorer care.

questions.stem: After a medication error by a junior doctor that did not harm the patient, which approach best reflects a just culture?

options.text: Ignore the event since there was no harm
Treat all errors as acceptable regardless of circumstances
Punish the doctor to deter others from making errors
Review the system factors that contributed, support the doctor to reflect and learn, and reserve disciplinary action for reckless behaviour

questions.correctOptionText: Review the system factors that contributed, support the doctor to reflect and learn, and reserve disciplinary action for reckless behaviour

distractorRationale.b: A just culture still holds people accountable for reckless behaviour.
distractorRationale.d: Correct: system focus with accountability where justified.

questions.explanation: A just culture looks first at how systems and workload contributed to an error, supports learning, and distinguishes honest mistakes from reckless or deliberate acts. Ignoring no-harm events or blaming individuals both reduce reporting and safety.

questions.stem: You prescribe an antibiotic for a patient and, 30 minutes later, realise from the allergy section of the chart that she has a documented severe allergic reaction to that antibiotic class. A nurse has not yet given it and the drug is cancelled. Describe what you would do next and the professional principles involved.
markingGuide: Confirms the prescription is stopped and the patient is safe, and checks no dose was given
Tells the nurse in charge and your supervisor promptly and honestly
Considers whether the patient should be told (professional duty of candour) in line with local policy and with senior advice
Reports the event, including as a near miss, using the incident system
Reflects on how the error happened (for example time pressure or the allergy not being visible) and records learning in the portfolio
Describes a just-culture approach, focusing on system causes such as alerts and chart design while accepting personal responsibility
Does not conceal the event or alter records
questions.explanation: Prompt disclosure and reporting of a near miss protect the patient and give the organisation a chance to fix the weakness. Credit goes for naming candour, the incident system, reflection and the focus on systems and personal accountability.

questions.stem: On a ward round a senior doctor tells you to give a dose of a drug that you believe is ten times higher than the dose in the BNF. What is the most appropriate response?

options.text: Quietly change the dose without telling anyone
Politely state your concern and ask the senior to check, do not give it until clarified, and escalate to another senior or pharmacist if it remains unresolved
Give the dose because the senior is more experienced
Say nothing and report it afterwards on the incident system

questions.correctOptionText: Politely state your concern and ask the senior to check, do not give it until clarified, and escalate to another senior or pharmacist if it remains unresolved

distractorRationale.a: Unilateral changes bypass communication and accountability.
distractorRationale.b: Correct: speaks up while protecting the patient.
distractorRationale.c: Compliance with a suspected error can harm patients.
distractorRationale.d: Reporting afterwards does not prevent the harm.

questions.explanation: Hierarchy must not stop a junior from speaking up about a possible error. A clear, respectful challenge with a request to check the reference source, escalation if needed and documentation protect the patient and preserve professional relationships.
